questions.statement: Which sentence about the morning bus is grammatically correct?
questions.context: A student in San Jose describes the schedule of the school bus that serves her town.

options.text: The bus from San Jose leaves Cartago at six in the morning.
options.feedback: Correct: the subject The bus is singular, and the present simple third person verb leaves agrees with it.

options.text: The students waiting at the stop is worried about the delay.
options.feedback: The subject The students waiting at the stop is plural, so the verb must be are worried, not is.

options.text: My brother works in Heredia and they studies engineering in the week.
options.feedback: They studies mixes a plural pronoun with a singular verb; it should be he studies or they study.

options.text: The teacher ask us to arrive before the school bell rings.
options.feedback: The teacher is third person singular, so the present simple needs asks instead of the base verb ask.

questions.explanation:
In the present simple a third person singular subject takes the -s ending, and a long modifier does not change whether the subject counts as one or many.

questions.statement: Which question tag agrees with the statement about the library?
questions.context: The new public library in Alajuela lends books and stays open late before exams.

options.text: We have to return the books on Friday, don't we?
options.feedback: A positive statement with have to needs the auxiliary have, so the tag must be haven't we, not don't we.

options.text: We have to return the books on Friday, hasn't it?
options.feedback: The pronoun it has no match in the statement, which is about we, so a tag built on it cannot agree.

options.text: We have to return the books on Friday, haven't we?
options.feedback: Correct: the tag copies the auxiliary have in the negative and keeps the pronoun we from the main clause.

options.text: We have to return the books on Friday, didn't they?
options.feedback: Didn't they is both negative and past, while the statement is positive and present, so the tag fails.

questions.explanation:
A question tag copies the auxiliary and the pronoun of the main clause and then reverses the polarity, so have to needs the tag haven't we.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is correct after the verb recommend?
questions.context: A school counsellor in Heredia advises a student about leaving a concert to catch the bus.

options.text: She recommended to take the bus early instead of staying for the concert.
options.feedback: After recommend the object is a gerund, so an infinitive beginning with to is not the pattern this verb takes.

options.text: She recommended taking the bus early instead of staying for the concert.
options.feedback: Correct: recommend takes a gerund object, so taking the bus is the natural and expected complement.

options.text: She recommended take the bus early instead of staying for the concert.
options.feedback: A bare base verb cannot follow recommend in this object position, because the object must be a noun or a gerund.

options.text: She recommended the taking of the bus early instead of staying for the concert.
options.feedback: This is a heavy nominalisation, while the plain gerund taking already carries the action and reads better.

questions.explanation:
Verbs such as recommend, suggest and enjoy are followed by a gerund or by a that clause, never by a to infinitive. Students often transfer the pattern of want or decide.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which passive version matches the active sentence about the clinic in Liberia?
questions.context: A reading passage in a grade 11 exam reports that a clinic in Liberia will take forty patients.

options.text: The clinic in Liberia will admit 40 patients on Monday.
options.feedback: This repeats the active sentence unchanged, so the be plus past participle structure never appears.

options.text: 40 patients will admit by the clinic in Liberia on Monday.
options.feedback: The verb admit is left active after the new subject, so the sentence does not form a passive at all.

options.text: 40 patients are admitted by the clinic in Liberia on Monday.
options.feedback: Are admitted is a present passive, but the active verb was future, so the tense shifts by mistake.

options.text: 40 patients will be admitted by the clinic in Liberia on Monday.
options.feedback: Correct: the object becomes the subject, will admit becomes will be admitted, and the agent follows by.

questions.explanation:
The passive makes the object the subject and uses be plus past participle, keeps the tense of the original verb, and adds the doer after by.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Sofia said, 'I am nervous about the exam.' How does she report it?
questions.context: Sofia, a student in Cartago, is preparing a presentation about her entrance exam.

options.text: She said that she was nervous about the exam.
options.feedback: Correct: reported speech shifts the tense one step back, so am becomes was and the pronoun changes to she.

options.text: She says that she is nervous about the exam.
options.feedback: Says and is keep the original tense and pronouns, so the sentence reads as a quotation rather than a report.

options.text: She said that she is nervous about the exam.
options.feedback: Said marks past reporting, but is was never shifted back, so the reported tense no longer matches the verb.

options.text: She told that she was nervous about the exam.
options.feedback: Tell requires a named object, as in told me, so it cannot be followed by a bare that clause here.

questions.explanation:
When the reporting verb is past, the tense inside the reported clause moves one step back: am becomes was, will becomes would, and pronouns also change.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Andres asked, 'What time does the library open?' How is it reported?
questions.context: At a high school in San Jose, Andres asked the librarian about her opening hours.

options.text: Andres asked what time did the library open.
options.feedback: A reported question takes statement word order, so no auxiliary do and no question mark survive in this clause.

options.text: Andres asked what time the library opened.
options.feedback: Correct: reported questions keep subject then verb, and does shifts back to the past tense opened.

options.text: Andres asked when does the library open.
options.feedback: The direct question word does stays in front of the auxiliary, so the clause is not converted at all.

options.text: Andres asked if what time the library opens.
options.feedback: The word if cannot introduce a what time word group, and the present tense opens was left unshifted.

questions.explanation:
A reported question uses statement word order and no question mark. If the main verb is past, the tense of the auxiliary inside the question also shifts back one step.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which relative word fits: 'The woman ___ organises our reading club lives in Alajuela'?
questions.context: A reading passage mentions the woman who organises the reading club of a school in Heredia.

options.text: which
options.feedback: Which refers to things, not to a person, so it cannot introduce the clause about the organiser.

options.text: where
options.feedback: Where needs a place as its object, but the clause describes what the woman does, not where she lives.

options.text: whose
options.feedback: Whose shows possession, as in whose club, and here the clause has no owner followed by a noun.

options.text: who
options.feedback: Correct: who refers to a person and is the natural relative pronoun before the verb organises.

questions.explanation:
Use who for people and which for things. Where replaces a place phrase and whose shows possession, so the meaning of the clause decides the word.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A student wrote: 'Each of the students have to bring two books.' Which fix is right?
questions.context: A student wrote a report about the book fair held at the college in San Jose.

options.text: Each of the students has to bring two books.
options.feedback: Correct: the subject of each is the singular pronoun it, so the verb takes the third person singular has.

options.text: Each of the students have to bring two books.
options.feedback: This repeats the original error, because have disagrees with the singular pronoun hidden inside each of.

options.text: Each of the student have to bring two books.
options.feedback: The noun is in the wrong number, since each needs the plural form students before the preposition of.

options.text: Every of the students has to bring two books.
options.feedback: Every cannot be followed by of the students, because every is already a determiner and does not allow that partitive.

questions.explanation:
In each of the students the real subject is the pronoun it, so the verb stays singular. The plural noun inside the phrase does not control the agreement.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which order of the three sentences makes logical sense in the passage?
questions.context: A reading text describes how a recycling programme changed a neighbourhood in Desamparados.

options.text: The stream turned clean. Braulio's team collected waste. It paid the workers.
options.feedback: The result appears before its causes, and the pronoun It then points at a team that has not been introduced.

options.text: Braulio's team paid the workers. The stream turned clean. It collected waste.
options.feedback: Payment comes before the collection that funds it, and It shifts its reference back to the team again.

options.text: Braulio's team collected waste. It paid the workers. The stream turned clean.
options.feedback: Correct: collection funds the payment, and the cleaning of the stream follows as the visible final result.

options.text: Braulio's team collected waste. The stream turned clean. It paid the workers.
options.feedback: The result arrives too early, and It after it refers to the stream, which cannot pay anybody.

questions.explanation:
A process text moves from action to action in a natural time order and keeps the pronoun it pointing at the same actor in each following sentence.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which second sentence keeps the pronoun reference clear for the reader?
questions.context: In a passage, the first sentence reads: 'The committee met the mayor on Tuesday.'

options.text: It had prepared a long list of questions about the new library.
options.feedback: It could point to the committee or to the mayor, so the reader cannot tell who wrote the questions.

options.text: They had prepared a long list of questions about the new library.
options.feedback: Correct: they matches the plural subject the committee and keeps the reference stable in the passage.

options.text: He had prepared a long list of questions about the new library.
options.feedback: He points to the mayor, which changes the actor and contradicts the reading that the committee prepared them.

options.text: This had prepared a long list of questions about the new library.
options.feedback: This cannot stand for a person or a group, so it breaks the agreement and the reference at once.

questions.explanation:
A pronoun must match the number of the noun it replaces and should keep that same referent. When two plural nouns compete, repeat the noun instead of guessing.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which structure is used in: 'Not until midnight did the storm reach Puntarenas'?
questions.context: A reading passage in a grade 11 exam describes a storm that reached Puntarenas at night.

options.text: The storm did not reach Puntarenas until it was at midnight.
options.feedback: This is a normal clause with the negative after the subject, so no inversion is present at all.

options.text: Until midnight the storm was reaching the town of Puntarenas.
options.feedback: The past continuous suggests an action in progress, but nothing here shows that progressive meaning.

options.text: Not until midnight did the storm reach Puntarenas.
options.feedback: Correct: after a negative adverbial at the start, the auxiliary did comes before the subject for emphasis.

options.text: The storm was not reaching Puntarenas until it was at midnight.
options.feedback: The progressive form was reaching suggests an ongoing action that the sentence never establishes.

questions.explanation:
A negative or restrictive adverbial placed at the front of a sentence triggers subject and auxiliary inversion, which gives the clause extra emphasis.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence describes a real regret about a situation that did not happen?
questions.context: Kevin from Alajuela is sorry that he missed the entrance exam preparation workshop.

options.text: If he had studied harder, he would have passed the entrance exam.
options.feedback: Correct: the third conditional pairs if plus had with would have, so it describes an unreal past situation.

options.text: If he studied harder, he would pass the entrance exam.
options.feedback: That is the second conditional, used for a present or future situation that is not real yet.

options.text: If he had studied harder, he would pass the entrance exam.
options.feedback: The tenses do not agree, because had plus would signals a mixed pair that no conditional form allows.

options.text: If he studies harder, he would have passed the entrance exam.
options.feedback: The present tense if clause cannot combine with the past perfect of would have, so the pair is ungrammatical.

questions.explanation:
The third conditional describes an unreal past and uses if plus past perfect with would plus have. The second conditional uses if plus past simple for unreal present or future.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence summarises a reading text without adding any new information?
questions.context: A test in San Jose asks students to choose the sentence that best summarises a reading text.

options.text: The new library in Alajuela also opened a small cinema next to the main hall.
options.feedback: The cinema is a new detail, and a summary must never introduce facts the passage did not contain.

options.text: Next year the council will probably build a second library in the town of Alajuela.
options.feedback: This is a prediction about the future, but a summary stays inside what the passage already said.

options.text: Some people in Alajuela think that the library should not have opened in May.
options.feedback: This reports another reader's opinion, which changes the voice of a summary from neutral to personal.

options.text: In short, the library opened in May to serve more students in the town.
options.feedback: Correct: it restates the opening and its purpose, adds nothing, and signals the summary with In short.

questions.explanation:
A summary sentence condenses the main point of a text in neutral language. It must not add facts, predictions or opinions that the original passage never expressed.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly completes the verb insist?
questions.context: Maria insisted on paying the whole dinner bill at a restaurant in Puntarenas.

options.text: Maria insisted on pay the whole dinner bill herself.
options.feedback: Insist takes the preposition on followed by a gerund, so a bare infinitive is not possible after it.

options.text: Maria insisted on paying the whole dinner bill herself.
options.feedback: Correct: insist on is a fixed phrase completed by a gerund, which is why paying follows the preposition.

options.text: Maria insisted in paying the whole dinner bill herself.
options.feedback: The preposition is wrong, because the idiom is insist on and no form of insist uses in this pattern.

options.text: Maria insisted paying on the whole dinner bill herself.
options.feedback: The gerund and the preposition are separated, and a gerund cannot be split from the preposition that governs it.

questions.explanation:
Insist on and insist that are the standard patterns. When a preposition follows the verb, it must be followed by a gerund, never by a bare or to infinitive.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the best formal version of 'They will announce the winners tomorrow'?
questions.context: A formal school report must state that the winners will be announced the next day.

options.text: The winners are going to be announce in the next day by them.
options.feedback: The passive is broken, because the participle announce must follow the auxiliary and never stand alone.

options.text: Tomorrow it is them who are going to announcing the winners.
options.feedback: The emphatic structure with them who requires a verb like will announce, and announcing after are is wrong.

options.text: The winners will be announced the following day.
options.feedback: Correct: the passive will be announced is complete, and the formal phrase the following day suits a report.

options.text: Tomorrow they are announcing the winners in a very official way.
options.feedback: The progressive are announcing suggests an action in progress, which the original sentence never states.

questions.explanation:
A formal version keeps the future passive, uses a past participle after the auxiliary and prefers a written time expression such as the following day.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which word best links the sentence to the reason that follows?
questions.context: A reading passage about a coffee farm near Turrialba mentions the workers who pick the beans.

options.text: In contrast, the workers only start at four in the morning.
options.feedback: In contrast signals opposition, but the sentence after it continues the same topic with no opposing idea.

options.text: On the other hand, the workers leave the farm before noon.
options.feedback: On the other hand also marks contrast, and no second view is set against the first one here.

options.text: Similarly, the workers take a bus from Turrialba every day.
options.feedback: Similarly adds a comparable point, which is not the relationship a following reason creates.

options.text: As a result, the workers rest in the shade during the hottest hours.
options.feedback: Correct: As a result introduces a consequence, and the rest in the shade is the outcome that follows.

questions.explanation:
A linking adverb must state the real relationship between two ideas. Result words follow a cause, contrast words oppose, and addition words simply add another point.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which passive is correct for: 'The nurse treated twelve patients yesterday'?
questions.context: A grammar test asks students to turn an active sentence about the Heredia clinic into the passive.

options.text: Twelve patients were treat by the nurse yesterday.
options.feedback: The passive needs a past participle, so treat after the auxiliary were leaves the structure unfinished.

options.text: Twelve patients were treated by the nurse yesterday.
options.feedback: Correct: the past participle treated follows the auxiliary were and the agent is added with by.

options.text: Twelve patients have been treated by the nurse yesterday.
options.feedback: The present perfect cannot stand with the finished time expression yesterday, which fixes the past.

options.text: Twelve patients were treating by the nurse yesterday.
options.feedback: Treating is a gerund or present participle and cannot fill the passive slot after the auxiliary were.

questions.explanation:
The passive pairs be in the same tense as the original verb with a past participle. Finished time expressions such as yesterday force the past simple, never the present perfect.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is correct when the condition is unlikely to happen?
questions.context: Diego from Liberia needs to describe a future plan that depends on a condition he does not control.

options.text: If the council approves the plan, we will paint the mural this weekend.
options.feedback: The first conditional uses if plus present and will, and it treats the approval as a real future possibility.

options.text: If the council approves the plan, we would paint the mural this weekend.
options.feedback: Mixing present if with would past breaks the pair, since the second conditional needs if plus past simple.

options.text: If the council approved the plan, we would paint the mural this weekend.
options.feedback: Correct: the third conditional pair if plus past simple with would describes a future action under an unlikely condition.

options.text: If the council will approve the plan, we would paint the mural this weekend.
options.feedback: An if clause never takes will or a future auxiliary, because the tense belongs to the main clause.

questions.explanation:
The third conditional uses if plus past simple with would for an unlikely or imagined future, while the first conditional keeps if plus present with will for realistic plans.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option keeps the tense and the time reference consistent in the report?
questions.context: A grade 11 student must keep a consistent tense across a report about a school trip to Monteverde.

options.text: Our class visited Monteverde in July, and we saw clouds below the bridge.
options.feedback: Correct: both clauses stay in the past simple, and the time word in July anchors both events to the trip.

options.text: Our class visits Monteverde in July and we saw clouds below the bridge.
options.feedback: Visits is present simple while saw is past, so the sentence jumps between two different time frames.

options.text: Our class visited Monteverde in July, and tomorrow we will see clouds below it.
options.feedback: The second clause moves to a future tomorrow, which breaks the single past reference set by visited in July.

options.text: Our class has visited Monteverde in July, so we are seeing the clouds now.
options.feedback: Has visited points to a finished event but are seeing suggests an action still in progress at the moment of writing.

questions.explanation:
A consistent tense keeps one time frame across linked clauses. When the context word fixes a finished past event, every clause should stay in the past simple.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which effect does putting a specific example right after a general claim have?
questions.context: A reading question asks what a text achieves by placing an example right after a general statement.

options.text: It proves the general claim, which no example can ever do.
options.feedback: An example supports and illustrates a claim, but it does not logically prove the claim for every case.

options.text: It delays the main idea until the very end of the paragraph.
options.feedback: The general claim comes first in this arrangement, so the main idea is not left hanging until the end.

options.text: It removes the need for any supporting detail in the rest of the text.
options.feedback: Details still matter after the example, since a paragraph usually needs more than one piece of support.

options.text: It makes the general claim concrete, so the reader can picture the situation.
options.feedback: Correct: an example turns an abstract statement into something the reader can picture and accept.

questions.explanation:
Writers follow a general claim with a specific example to make the abstract idea concrete. Support strengthens a claim; it never replaces the need for further detail.
